claims.text: The baseline material is HfZrTiTa0.53 in an as-solutionized or as-cast state.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a baseline yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has a baseline compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain is a baseline uniform tensile elongation for HfZrTiTa0.53.
Aging HfZrTiTa0.53 at 600°C for 1 hour followed by rapid quenching will form nanoscale Hf-rich precipitates.
The precipitates produced by the treatment will be uniformly distributed.
The Hf-rich precipitates will occur both within the matrix and along grain boundaries.
Tight control of aging time and quench rate will prevent precipitate coarsening.
Finely dispersed Hf-rich precipitates will act as barriers to dislocation motion and accumulation.
The precipitate barrier effect will promote distributed plasticity.
Distributed plasticity will delay tensile necking.
The treatment will increase uniform tensile elongation by approximately 40–50% relative to 13.5%.
After treatment, yield strength will remain near 786 MPa.
After treatment, compressive strength will remain near 1314 MPa.
After treatment, impact-triggered chemical energy release will remain equivalent to the baseline.
Precipitate coarsening can cause embrittlement in the treated alloy.
The predicted behavior applies at approximately 25°C and a quasi-static tensile strain rate of about 10^-3 s^-1.
The hypothesis may not hold after elevated-temperature exposure or when process deviations produce precipitate coarsening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis places all mechanical tests at a quasi-static strain rate of about 10^-3 s^-1 while also requiring impact tests. Impact-triggered energy-release testing is dynamic, so a single quasi-static limit cannot coherently describe both the tensile/compression tests and the impact test.
